common_name: Avondale Chinese Redbud (Intense Rose-Purple Compact Redbud)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Avondale stays more compact and shrubby than the species and is notably more shade-tolerant than Eastern redbud, making it well suited to smaller gardens and understory positions.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the multi-stemmed shrub room to develop its dense, rounded form. Avondale is a New Zealand selection of Chinese redbud prized for producing the most intensely colored bloom of any redbud in general cultivation, with deep rose-purple to magenta pea flowers packed so densely along every branch, twig, and even the older trunk wood that the bare stems all but disappear under the spring flower display. Its naturally compact, shrubby habit stays smaller and tidier than the species, and its greater shade tolerance compared with Eastern redbud makes it a strong choice for a woodland-edge planting, foundation bed, or small-garden specimen where its eye-level bloom show can be appreciated up close. Large, glossy heart-shaped leaves follow the flowers and turn clear yellow in fall; prune only to remove dead or crossing wood right after bloom.

common_name: Max Frei Cranesbill (Compact Magenta Bloody Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Max Frei is a compact selection of bloody cranesbill that stays notably lower and tighter than the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, where too-rich soil or too much shade leads to looser, floppier growth. Max Frei forms a low, dense, tidy mound of finely cut, deep green leaves smothered in bright magenta-pink flowers with darker veining through late spring and into summer, more compact and floriferous than the wild species. Its low, spreading habit and tolerance of poor, dry soil make it a dependable edging plant, rock garden subject, or front-of-border filler that needs almost no maintenance beyond an optional light shearing after the first flush to tidy the mound and encourage a smaller rebloom. Foliage often takes on attractive red-orange fall color before dying back for winter, and established clumps are long-lived, rarely needing division except to propagate new plants.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Biokovo spreads steadily by rhizome to form a dense weed-suppressing mat and tolerates dry shade better than most flowering groundcovers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun, and water regularly the first season while the rhizomes spread and knit the planting into a solid mat. Biokovo is a hybrid cranesbill named for a mountain range in Croatia, forming a low, dense, semi-evergreen carpet of aromatic, lobed leaves that turn attractive orange-red tones in fall, topped in late spring by a heavy flush of small, white flowers delicately blushed with pink at the base of each petal. It is among the most reliable and low-maintenance flowering groundcovers available, tolerating dry shade, poor soil, heat, and drought far better than most perennials grown for groundcover use, and it resists deer and rabbit browsing thanks to its scented foliage. An occasional light shearing after bloom keeps the mat tidy, but otherwise it needs no regular care beyond dividing overgrown patches every several years to control spread or propagate new plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Himalayan geranium spreads gently by rhizome to form a loose, weaving groundcover rather than staying in a tight clump.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and provide afternoon shade and even moisture where summers are hot. Native to the Himalayas and Central Asia, Geranium himalayense forms a loose, spreading mound of deeply lobed, softly hairy leaves and bears large, saucer-shaped, violet-blue flowers with darker veining and a small white eye through late spring and early summer. It weaves attractively among neighboring perennials without becoming aggressive, and its rich blue flower color is among the truest blues found in hardy geraniums, making it a valuable companion for pink- and yellow-flowered border plants. Cut the plant back hard after its main flush to tidy the foliage and often coax a lighter rebloom later in the season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to keep growth vigorous.

common_name: Weyer's Butterfly Bush (Orange-Gold Globe-Flowered Buddleja Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; this hybrid butterfly bush blooms on new wood, so an annual hard cutback in late winter keeps it compact and encourages the heaviest flowering.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, and cut the entire shrub back hard, to within a foot or so of the ground, in late winter each year, since flowers form on new growth and a severe annual pruning keeps the shrub compact and floriferous rather than large and leggy. Buddleja x weyeriana is a cross between the familiar purple butterfly bush (B. davidii) and the yellow-flowered B. globosa, combining the long, arching bloom season of the former with rounded, ball-shaped flower clusters closer to the latter, opening in shades of warm orange, gold, and apricot from midsummer through fall. Like other butterfly bushes it is a magnet for butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds, and its distinctive globe-shaped flower clusters and unusual color range set it apart from the more common purple- and pink-flowered Buddleja davidii cultivars. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, and deadheading spent flower clusters through the season helps prolong the bloom display.
